Overview: A mental health condition characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks—sudden periods of intense fear that may include heart palpitations, sweating, shortness of breath, or feelings of impending doom.
Causes: Exact cause is not fully understood. Likely involves a combination of genetic factors, brain chemistry, stress, and environmental influences.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Common treatments include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), medications such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), and lifestyle changes like stress management.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing frequent panic attacks, persistent fear of future attacks, or symptoms that interfere with daily life.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), Mayo Clinic

Overview: A noncancerous growth on a vocal cord that can affect voice quality, often causing hoarseness.
Causes: Usually caused by vocal strain or trauma (such as excessive talking, shouting, or singing), irritation from smoking, or acid reflux.
Prevention: Avoid vocal strain, stay hydrated, avoid smoking, and manage acid reflux.
Treatment: Voice therapy, lifestyle changes, and in some cases surgical removal.
When to see a doctor: If hoarseness or voice changes last longer than 2–3 weeks.
Sources: American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery, Mayo Clinic

Overview: A genetic condition affecting females in which one of the X chromosomes is missing or partially missing, leading to developmental and medical challenges.
Causes: Caused by complete or partial absence of one X chromosome (monosomy X).
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Growth hormone therapy, estrogen replacement therapy, and management of associated health issues (such as heart or kidney problems).
When to see a doctor: Typically diagnosed in childhood; evaluation is needed if there is short stature, delayed puberty, or characteristic physical features.
Sources: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Mayo Clinic, Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center (GARD)

Overview: A condition in which one or both testicles fail to descend into the scrotum before birth.
Causes: Exact cause is unclear; may involve hormonal, genetic, and environmental factors affecting fetal development.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Often resolves on its own in infancy; if not, surgery (orchiopexy) is typically performed.
When to see a doctor: If a testicle is not in the scrotum by 6 months of age.
Sources: American Urological Association, Mayo Clinic

Overview: A toxic condition caused by ingestion of ethylene glycol, a chemical found in antifreeze, leading to metabolic acidosis and organ damage, especially the kidneys.
Causes: Ingestion of substances containing ethylene glycol.
Prevention: Store chemicals safely, use child-proof containers, and avoid ingestion of unknown liquids.
Treatment: Emergency treatment includes administration of antidotes (such as fomepizole), supportive care, and possibly dialysis.
When to see a doctor: Immediately after suspected ingestion or symptoms such as confusion, vomiting, or difficulty breathing.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Poison Control Center, Mayo Clinic

Overview: A condition involving thinning, drying, and inflammation of the vaginal walls due to decreased estrogen levels, most commonly after menopause.
Causes: Reduced estrogen levels, typically due to menopause, but can also occur after childbirth, during breastfeeding, or as a result of certain medications or cancer treatments.
Prevention: Regular sexual activity, use of vaginal moisturizers, and in some cases estrogen therapy may help reduce risk.
Treatment: Vaginal moisturizers and lubricants, local or systemic estrogen therapy, and other prescribed medications depending on severity.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing vaginal dryness, itching, burning, pain during intercourse, or unusual discharge that affects quality of life.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: A break in one or more of the bones in the hand, including the metacarpals or phalanges, often caused by trauma.
Causes: Direct impact, falls, sports injuries, or accidents that apply force to the hand.
Prevention: Using protective gear during activities, practicing safety measures, and maintaining bone health.
Treatment: Immobilization with splints or casts, pain management, and in some cases surgical repair.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe pain, swelling, deformity, inability to move the hand, or suspected fracture after injury.
Sources: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Mayo Clinic

Overview: A bacterial infection in the tissues of the mouth that can cause swelling, redness, pain, and sometimes pus formation (abscess).
Causes: Bacterial infection often resulting from untreated dental decay, gum disease, or injury to oral tissues.
Prevention: Good oral hygiene, regular dental check-ups, and prompt treatment of dental issues.
Treatment: Antibiotics, drainage of abscess if present, and dental treatment of the underlying cause.
When to see a doctor: If there is swelling, severe pain, fever, difficulty swallowing, or spreading infection.
Sources: American Dental Association, Mayo Clinic

Overview: A condition in which the eyes do not align properly with each other, often referred to as strabismus, which can affect vision and depth perception.
Causes: Problems with eye muscles, nerve signals, or brain control of eye movement; may be congenital or acquired.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Eyeglasses, vision therapy, eye patches, or surgery depending on severity and cause.
When to see a doctor: If there is noticeable eye misalignment, double vision, or difficulty focusing.
Sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Mayo Clinic

Overview: A common complication following a lumbar puncture (spinal tap), characterized by a headache that worsens when sitting or standing and improves when lying down.
Causes: Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the puncture site, leading to decreased pressure around the brain.
Prevention: Using proper needle technique and smaller needles may reduce risk, but it cannot always be prevented.
Treatment: Rest, hydration, caffeine, pain relievers, and in persistent cases, an epidural blood patch.
When to see a doctor: If the headache is severe, persistent, or accompanied by symptoms like nausea, vomiting, or neurological changes.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: A condition in infants where the pylorus (the passage from the stomach to the small intestine) becomes abnormally thickened, blocking food from entering the intestine.
Causes: Exact cause is not fully understood; likely involves a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Surgical procedure called pyloromyotomy to relieve the obstruction, along with fluid and electrolyte correction.
When to see a doctor: If an infant has forceful (projectile) vomiting, persistent hunger, dehydration, or weight loss.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: A group of conditions affecting the salivary glands, including infections, blockages, tumors, or autoimmune diseases that impact saliva production.
Causes: May include infections, salivary stones, autoimmune conditions (such as Sjögren’s syndrome), or tumors.
Prevention: Good oral hygiene and staying hydrated may help reduce risk of some types.
Treatment: Depends on cause; may include antibiotics, hydration, gland massage, removal of stones, or surgery.
When to see a doctor: If there is persistent swelling, pain, dry mouth, difficulty swallowing, or signs of infection.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Dental Association

Overview: A group of disorders that affect bone growth in children and adolescents, involving the degeneration and subsequent regeneration of bone and cartilage.
Causes: Not fully understood; may involve repetitive stress, reduced blood supply to bone, and genetic factors.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Rest, physical therapy, pain management, and in some cases bracing or surgery.
When to see a doctor: If a child or adolescent has persistent joint pain, swelling, or limited movement.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons

Overview: Damage to structures of the knee such as ligaments, tendons, cartilage, or bones, often due to trauma or overuse.
Causes: Sports injuries, falls, sudden twisting motions, or direct impact.
Prevention: Proper training, strengthening exercises, protective gear, and avoiding overuse.
Treatment: Rest, ice, compression, elevation (RICE), physical therapy, medications, and sometimes surgery.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe pain, swelling, instability, inability to bear weight, or deformity.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons

Overview: A broad group of conditions that disrupt normal metabolism, affecting how the body converts food into energy or processes specific substances.
Causes: May be genetic (inherited enzyme deficiencies) or acquired due to disease, lifestyle, or environmental factors.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Varies widely depending on the specific disorder; may include dietary management, medications, or enzyme replacement therapy.
When to see a doctor: If there are unexplained symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, developmental issues, or abnormal lab results.
Sources: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Mayo Clinic

Overview: Inflammation of the vagina that can result in discharge, itching, pain, or odor, often caused by infection or imbalance of vaginal flora.
Causes: Bacterial infections (bacterial vaginosis), yeast infections (Candida), parasites (such as Trichomonas), hormonal changes, or irritants.
Prevention: Good hygiene, avoiding irritants (such as scented products), safe sexual practices, and wearing breathable clothing.
Treatment: Depends on cause; may include antifungal medications, antibiotics, or antiparasitic drugs.
When to see a doctor: If there is unusual discharge, strong odor, itching, burning, or discomfort.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Overview: A group of heart rhythm disorders caused by malfunction of the sinus node, leading to irregular heartbeats such as bradycardia, pauses, or alternating fast and slow rhythms.
Causes: Age-related degeneration of the sinus node, heart disease, or damage to heart tissue; sometimes medication-related.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: May include medications or implantation of a pacemaker to regulate heart rhythm.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing dizziness, fainting, fatigue, palpitations, or shortness of breath.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Heart Association

Overview: A condition characterized by the perception of ringing or other noises in the ears without an external sound source, with no clearly identifiable underlying cause.
Causes: I don't know
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Management strategies may include sound therapy, hearing aids, counseling, and coping techniques.
When to see a doctor: If tinnitus is persistent, worsening, or associated with hearing loss, dizziness, or other symptoms.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD)

Overview: A group of eye conditions that damage the optic nerve, often associated with increased intraocular pressure, potentially leading to vision loss.
Causes: Often related to increased pressure in the eye due to fluid buildup; can also occur with normal pressure (normal-tension glaucoma).
Prevention: Regular eye exams may help detect it early; other preventive measures are limited.
Treatment: Eye drops, oral medications, laser therapy, or surgery to reduce intraocular pressure.
When to see a doctor: Regular eye exams are important; immediate care is needed for sudden vision changes, severe eye pain, or halos around lights.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Ophthalmology

Overview: Eating disorders are mental health conditions involving persistent disturbances in eating behavior, body image, weight concerns and emotional regulation. They may include restrictive eating, binge eating, purging, fear of weight gain, avoidance of food or excessive concern about body shape. These disorders can affect physical health, mood, social relationships and daily functioning.
Causes: Possible causes include genetic vulnerability, anxiety, depression, perfectionism, low self-esteem, traumatic experiences, social pressure related to body image, extreme dieting, family factors and cultural pressure around weight and appearance.
Prevention: Prevention may include promoting healthy body image, avoiding extreme diets, encouraging balanced eating habits, reducing weight-related teasing, addressing anxiety or depression early, supporting self-esteem and educating families about warning signs.
Treatment: Treatment may include psychotherapy, nutritional counseling, medical monitoring, family support and sometimes medication for associated anxiety or depression. Care is often multidisciplinary and may involve a doctor, psychologist, psychiatrist and dietitian.
When to see a doctor: Seek medical help if there is rapid weight loss, fainting, frequent vomiting, severe restriction of food, dehydration, irregular heartbeat, chest pain, suicidal thoughts, loss of menstrual periods or if eating behaviors interfere with daily life.
Sources: National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), Mayo Clinic

Overview: A temporary period of neurological symptoms caused by reduced blood flow to part of the brain, often called a 'mini-stroke', without permanent damage.
Causes: Temporary blockage of blood flow to the brain, often due to a blood clot or narrowed arteries.
Prevention: Managing risk factors such as high blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, and avoiding smoking.
Treatment: Medications to prevent blood clots (such as antiplatelets), lifestyle changes, and sometimes surgical procedures.
When to see a doctor: Immediately if experiencing stroke-like symptoms such as weakness, speech difficulty, or vision problems, even if they resolve quickly.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Stroke Association

Overview: A type of urinary tract infection that affects the kidneys, potentially causing serious illness if untreated.
Causes: Bacterial infection, often spreading from the lower urinary tract (bladder) to the kidneys.
Prevention: Staying hydrated, practicing good hygiene, and treating urinary tract infections promptly.
Treatment: Antibiotics, and in severe cases hospitalization with intravenous fluids and medications.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing fever, back or side pain, nausea, vomiting, or urinary symptoms such as burning or frequent urination.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: Damage to the group of muscles and tendons that stabilize the shoulder joint, often causing pain and limited movement.
Causes: Acute injury, repetitive overhead motions, or age-related degeneration.
Prevention: Strengthening shoulder muscles, proper technique during activities, and avoiding repetitive strain.
Treatment: Rest, physical therapy, medications, corticosteroid injections, and sometimes surgery.
When to see a doctor: If shoulder pain persists, limits movement, or worsens over time.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons

Overview: A condition characterized by persistent pain lasting longer than expected healing time, often affecting physical and psychological well-being.
Causes: May result from injury, illness, or unknown factors; can involve nervous system sensitization.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Multimodal approach including medications, physical therapy, psychological therapy, and lifestyle changes.
When to see a doctor: If pain persists for months, interferes with daily activities, or is associated with emotional distress.
Sources: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Mayo Clinic

Overview: A broad category referring to complications that may occur during pregnancy, affecting the health of the mother, fetus, or both.
Causes: I don't know
Prevention: Regular prenatal care, healthy lifestyle, and managing existing medical conditions.
Treatment: Varies widely depending on the specific condition or complication.
When to see a doctor: Regular prenatal visits are essential; immediate care is needed for symptoms like severe pain, bleeding, decreased fetal movement, or high blood pressure symptoms.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Mayo Clinic

Overview: A type of cancer that begins in the cells of the liver, most commonly hepatocellular carcinoma.
Causes: Chronic liver diseases such as hepatitis B or C infection, cirrhosis, alcohol-related liver disease, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
Prevention: Vaccination against hepatitis B, reducing alcohol consumption, maintaining a healthy weight, and avoiding exposure to hepatitis viruses.
Treatment: Depends on stage; may include surgery, liver transplant, ablation therapies, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing unexplained weight loss, loss of appetite, upper abdominal pain, jaundice, or fatigue.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Cancer Institute

Overview: A condition in which part or all of a lung collapses or does not fully inflate, leading to reduced oxygen exchange.
Causes: Blockage of airways (such as mucus plugs or tumors) or pressure from outside the lung (such as fluid, air, or tumors).
Prevention: Deep breathing exercises after surgery, avoiding prolonged immobility, and managing underlying lung conditions.
Treatment: Depends on cause; may include breathing exercises, chest physiotherapy, medications, or procedures to remove blockage.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing difficulty breathing, rapid breathing, or low oxygen levels.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: Damage to the structures of the hand, including bones, ligaments, tendons, or soft tissues, often due to trauma.
Causes: Falls, direct impact, cuts, crush injuries, or repetitive strain.
Prevention: Using protective equipment, practicing safety measures, and avoiding hazardous activities.
Treatment: Rest, ice, compression, elevation (RICE), wound care, immobilization, and in some cases surgery.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe pain, swelling, deformity, loss of function, numbness, or deep wounds.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons

Overview: The presence of gallstones in the common bile duct, which can block the flow of bile.
Causes: Gallstones formed in the gallbladder that migrate into the bile duct.
Prevention: Maintaining a healthy weight, balanced diet, and managing risk factors for gallstones.
Treatment: Endoscopic removal of stones (ERCP), surgery, or other procedures to restore bile flow.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing jaundice, abdominal pain, fever, or signs of infection.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: Damage to the hip joint or surrounding structures, including bones, muscles, ligaments, or tendons.
Causes: Falls, accidents, sports injuries, or overuse.
Prevention: Strengthening exercises, balance training, and using protective measures to prevent falls.
Treatment: Rest, physical therapy, medications, and in severe cases surgery.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe pain, inability to move or bear weight, swelling, or deformity.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons

Overview: A condition where blood flow to the intestines is reduced, leading to tissue damage and potential necrosis.
Causes: Blocked or narrowed blood vessels due to clots, atherosclerosis, or low blood flow states.
Prevention: Managing cardiovascular risk factors such as high blood pressure, cholesterol, and avoiding smoking.
Treatment: Emergency treatment may include medications, procedures to restore blood flow, or surgery to remove damaged tissue.
When to see a doctor: Immediate medical attention is needed for sudden severe abdominal pain, bloody stools, or signs of shock.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: A condition in a child resulting from alcohol exposure during pregnancy, leading to physical, behavioral, and learning problems.
Causes: Alcohol consumption during pregnancy.
Prevention: Avoiding alcohol during pregnancy.
Treatment: No cure; management includes supportive care, educational support, and therapy.
When to see a doctor: If developmental delays, learning difficulties, or characteristic facial features are noticed in a child.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA)

Overview: Inflammation of the peritoneum, the tissue lining the inner wall of the abdomen and covering abdominal organs, often due to infection.
Causes: Bacterial or fungal infection, commonly from a ruptured organ such as the appendix, stomach, or intestines.
Prevention: Prompt treatment of abdominal infections and medical conditions.
Treatment: Emergency treatment with antibiotics and often surgery to treat the underlying cause.
When to see a doctor: Immediate care is needed for severe abdominal pain, fever, nausea, or abdominal tenderness.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: Damage to the abdominal area involving organs, muscles, or blood vessels, often due to trauma.
Causes: Blunt force trauma, accidents, falls, or penetrating injuries.
Prevention: Using seatbelts, protective gear, and practicing safety measures.
Treatment: Depends on severity; may include monitoring, medications, or surgery.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe pain, bruising, bleeding, vomiting, or signs of internal injury.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American College of Surgeons

Overview: A sudden inflammation of the pancreas that can range from mild discomfort to a life-threatening illness.
Causes: Gallstones, heavy alcohol use, high triglycerides, certain medications, or infections.
Prevention: Limiting alcohol intake, maintaining a healthy diet, and managing risk factors such as gallstones.
Treatment: Hospital care with fluids, pain control, and treatment of the underlying cause.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or fever.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: Inflammation of a vein caused by a blood clot, commonly occurring in the legs.
Causes: Blood clots due to prolonged immobility, injury to a vein, or clotting disorders.
Prevention: Staying active, avoiding prolonged immobility, and using compression stockings if at risk.
Treatment: Warm compresses, anti-inflammatory medications, blood thinners, and compression therapy.
When to see a doctor: If there is pain, swelling, redness along a vein, or symptoms suggesting a deep vein clot.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: A chronic respiratory condition characterized by inflammation and narrowing of the airways, leading to difficulty breathing.
Causes: Combination of genetic and environmental factors, including allergens, infections, and irritants.
Prevention: Avoiding known triggers, using preventive medications, and managing allergies.
Treatment: Inhaled medications such as bronchodilators and corticosteroids, along with long-term control therapy.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing frequent wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, or asthma attacks.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Overview: A condition where an object is present inside the vagina, which may cause irritation, infection, or discharge.
Causes: Insertion of objects such as tampons, contraceptive devices, or other items that are retained or forgotten.
Prevention: Proper use and timely removal of vaginal products and avoiding insertion of inappropriate objects.
Treatment: Removal of the foreign body by a healthcare professional and treatment of any resulting infection.
When to see a doctor: If there is unusual discharge, foul odor, pain, bleeding, or suspicion of a retained object.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

Overview: A neurological disorder characterized by an uncontrollable urge to move the legs, usually due to uncomfortable sensations, often worsening at night.
Causes: Not fully understood; may involve genetic factors, iron deficiency, or underlying medical conditions.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Lifestyle changes, iron supplementation if deficient, and medications to manage symptoms.
When to see a doctor: If symptoms interfere with sleep or daily activities.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)

Overview: A chronic lung condition in which the air sacs (alveoli) are damaged, leading to shortness of breath.
Causes: Long-term exposure to airborne irritants, especially cigarette smoke.
Prevention: Avoid smoking and exposure to air pollutants and occupational irritants.
Treatment: Medications, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen therapy, and in some cases surgery.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing persistent shortness of breath, chronic cough, or wheezing.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Overview: A parasitic infection caused by the larval form of the pork tapeworm, which can affect tissues such as muscles, eyes, and the brain.
Causes: Ingestion of eggs of the parasite (Taenia solium), typically through contaminated food or water.
Prevention: Proper hygiene, safe food handling, and avoiding contaminated food and water.
Treatment: Antiparasitic medications, anti-inflammatory drugs, and sometimes surgery depending on location and severity.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing seizures, headaches, or neurological symptoms.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), World Health Organization (WHO)

Overview: A medical or surgical procedure to end a pregnancy.
Causes: I don't know
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: I don't know
When to see a doctor: Follow-up care is typically recommended after the procedure or if complications such as heavy bleeding, severe pain, or fever occur.
Sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Mayo Clinic

Overview: A condition associated with the eruption of primary teeth in infants, sometimes linked to mild discomfort, irritability, and gum swelling.
Causes: Eruption of teeth through the gums.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Teething rings, gentle gum massage, and in some cases mild pain relief as recommended by a healthcare provider.
When to see a doctor: If there is high fever, severe symptoms, or concerns beyond typical teething discomfort.
Sources: American Academy of Pediatrics, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Inflammation of the stomach and intestines caused by infection, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps.
Causes: Viruses (such as norovirus or rotavirus), bacteria, or parasites.
Prevention: Good hygiene, safe food handling, clean water, and vaccination (e.g., rotavirus vaccine in children).
Treatment: Hydration, rest, and in some cases medications depending on the cause.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, high fever, or blood in stool.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Mayo Clinic

Overview: A short-term inflammation of the sinuses, often following a cold, causing nasal congestion, facial pain, and discharge.
Causes: Usually viral infections; sometimes bacterial infections.
Prevention: Hand hygiene, avoiding upper respiratory infections, and managing allergies.
Treatment: Symptomatic relief (decongestants, pain relievers), and in some cases antibiotics if bacterial.
When to see a doctor: If symptoms last more than 10 days, worsen, or include high fever or severe facial pain.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Overview: A group of mental health conditions related to the misuse of substances such as alcohol or drugs, affecting mood, behavior, and cognition.
Causes: Use or withdrawal of substances, along with genetic, psychological, and environmental factors.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Behavioral therapy, medications, detoxification programs, and support groups.
When to see a doctor: If substance use is causing problems in daily life, health, or relationships.
Sources: National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), Mayo Clinic

Overview: A type of depression that occurs after childbirth, affecting mood, energy, and ability to care for the baby.
Causes: Hormonal changes, emotional factors, sleep deprivation, and personal or family history of depression.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Psychotherapy, medications such as antidepressants, and support from healthcare providers and family.
When to see a doctor: If feelings of sadness, hopelessness, or anxiety persist, worsen, or interfere with daily functioning.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

Overview: A condition where plaque builds up in the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.
Causes: Accumulation of cholesterol and other substances in artery walls, often linked to high cholesterol, smoking, high blood pressure, and diabetes.
Prevention: Healthy diet, regular exercise, avoiding smoking, and managing blood pressure and cholesterol.
Treatment: Lifestyle changes, medications, and procedures such as angioplasty or bypass surgery.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing chest pain, shortness of breath, or other signs of heart disease.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Heart Association

Overview: Inflammation of the vertebrae in the spine, which can lead to pain and stiffness; may be part of conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis.
Causes: Inflammatory conditions, autoimmune factors, or infections.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Medications to reduce inflammation, physical therapy, and lifestyle management.
When to see a doctor: If there is persistent back pain, stiffness, or reduced mobility.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: A usually benign tumor of the pituitary gland that can affect hormone production.
Causes: Exact cause is not well understood; may involve genetic factors in some cases.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Observation, medications, surgery, or radiation therapy depending on type and size.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing vision problems, headaches, or symptoms of hormone imbalance.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: Noncancerous growths of the uterus that often appear during childbearing years.
Causes: Exact cause is not known; influenced by hormones (estrogen and progesterone) and possibly genetic factors.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Medications to manage symptoms, hormonal therapy, noninvasive procedures, or surgery depending on severity.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain, frequent urination, or difficulty emptying the bladder.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: Abnormal vaginal bleeding that occurs outside of regular menstrual periods with no identified cause.
Causes: I don't know
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Depends on evaluation findings; may include hormonal therapy or monitoring.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing unexpected or persistent vaginal bleeding outside of normal periods.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

Overview: A small, painless lump or swelling on the eyelid caused by a blocked oil gland.
Causes: Blockage of a meibomian gland in the eyelid, sometimes associated with inflammation.
Prevention: Good eyelid hygiene and managing conditions like blepharitis.
Treatment: Warm compresses, gentle massage, and in some cases minor surgery or medication.
When to see a doctor: If the lump persists, grows, affects vision, or becomes painful.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Ophthalmology

Overview: A medical emergency in which an ovary twists around the ligaments that support it, cutting off blood supply.
Causes: Often associated with ovarian cysts or masses that make the ovary more likely to twist.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Emergency surgery to untwist or remove the affected ovary.
When to see a doctor: Immediate care is needed for sudden, severe lower abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

disease_name: Retinopathy due to high blood pressure
Overview: Damage to the blood vessels of the retina caused by chronic high blood pressure.
Causes: Long-standing hypertension damaging retinal vessels.
Prevention: Controlling blood pressure through lifestyle changes and medication.
Treatment: Managing blood pressure and treating complications as needed.
When to see a doctor: Regular eye exams are important; seek care if vision changes occur.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Eye Institute

Overview: A common fungal infection of the vagina that causes itching, irritation, and discharge.
Causes: Overgrowth of Candida fungus, often due to antibiotic use, hormonal changes, or weakened immune system.
Prevention: Keeping the genital area dry, avoiding irritants, and wearing breathable clothing.
Treatment: Antifungal medications (topical or oral).
When to see a doctor: If symptoms are severe, recurrent, or unclear.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Overview: A serious bacterial infection of the mastoid bone located behind the ear, often resulting from untreated ear infections.
Causes: Spread of middle ear infection to the mastoid bone.
Prevention: Prompt treatment of ear infections.
Treatment: Antibiotics and sometimes surgery.
When to see a doctor: If there is ear pain, swelling behind the ear, fever, or drainage from the ear.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: A bruise of the lung tissue caused by chest trauma, leading to bleeding and swelling that can impair oxygen exchange.
Causes: Blunt chest trauma such as car accidents, falls, or sports injuries.
Prevention: Using seatbelts, protective gear, and following safety precautions.
Treatment: Supportive care including oxygen therapy, pain management, and monitoring; severe cases may require ventilation.
When to see a doctor: Immediately after chest injury or if experiencing difficulty breathing, chest pain, or coughing up blood.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American College of Surgeons

Overview: A genetic heart condition in which the heart muscle becomes abnormally thickened, obstructing blood flow out of the heart.
Causes: Genetic mutations affecting heart muscle proteins.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Medications, lifestyle adjustments, procedures to reduce obstruction, or implantable devices.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, or palpitations.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Heart Association

Overview: A condition where the edge of a toenail grows into the surrounding skin, causing pain, redness, and swelling.
Causes: Improper nail trimming, tight footwear, injury, or genetic factors.
Prevention: Proper nail trimming, wearing comfortable shoes, and maintaining foot hygiene.
Treatment: Warm soaks, proper nail care, antibiotics if infected, and in severe cases minor surgery.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe pain, infection, or if the condition recurs.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Podiatric Medical Association

Overview: A group of conditions characterized by increased eosinophils (a type of white blood cell) in the lungs, leading to inflammation.
Causes: Allergic reactions, infections (especially parasitic), medications, or unknown causes.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Corticosteroids and treatment of the underlying cause.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing cough, fever, shortness of breath, or unexplained respiratory symptoms.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: A broad category of conditions affecting the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye, which can impact vision.
Causes: Infections, injuries, genetic conditions, or degenerative diseases.
Prevention: Protecting the eyes, proper contact lens hygiene, and regular eye care.
Treatment: Depends on cause; may include medications, corrective lenses, or surgery.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing eye pain, redness, blurred vision, or sensitivity to light.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Ophthalmology

disease_name: Foreign body in the gastrointestinal tract
Overview: A condition where an object is swallowed and becomes lodged somewhere in the digestive tract.
Causes: Accidental or intentional ingestion of objects.
Prevention: Keeping small objects out of reach of children and avoiding ingestion of non-food items.
Treatment: Observation if the object passes naturally, or endoscopic or surgical removal if needed.
When to see a doctor: If there is difficulty swallowing, abdominal pain, vomiting, or suspected ingestion of a dangerous object.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy

Overview: A severe inflammation of the interior of the eye, usually due to infection, which can threaten vision.
Causes: Infection following eye surgery, injury, or spread from another part of the body.
Prevention: Proper sterile techniques during eye procedures and prompt treatment of eye injuries.
Treatment: Emergency treatment with antibiotics or antifungal medications, sometimes surgery.
When to see a doctor: Immediate care is needed for eye pain, vision loss, redness, or sensitivity to light.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American Academy of Ophthalmology

Overview: A condition where the small intestine cannot properly absorb nutrients from food.
Causes: Various conditions such as celiac disease, infections, pancreatic insufficiency, or inflammatory bowel disease.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Depends on cause; may include dietary changes, supplements, or medications.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing chronic diarrhea, weight loss, or nutritional deficiencies.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, National Institutes of Health (NIH)

Overview: Noncancerous skin growths caused by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV).
Causes: Infection with HPV through direct contact or contaminated surfaces.
Prevention: Avoiding direct contact with warts, maintaining good hygiene, and protecting skin from cuts.
Treatment: Topical treatments, cryotherapy, or other removal methods.
When to see a doctor: If warts are painful, spreading, or do not respond to treatment.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Overview: A condition characterized by excessive sweating beyond what is necessary for normal temperature regulation. It commonly affects areas such as the palms, soles, underarms, and face, and can significantly impact daily activities and social interactions.
Causes: Primary hyperhidrosis has no clear cause and is thought to involve overactivity of sweat glands, possibly influenced by genetics. Secondary hyperhidrosis can result from medical conditions such as endocrine disorders, infections, or medication side effects.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Treatment options include prescription-strength antiperspirants, medications that reduce sweating, iontophoresis, botulinum toxin injections, and in severe cases surgical procedures.
When to see a doctor: If sweating disrupts daily life, occurs during sleep, or is accompanied by symptoms such as weight loss, fever, or chest pain.
Sources: International Hyperhidrosis Society, National Health Service (NHS), Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A serious medical condition that occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted or reduced, preventing brain tissue from receiving oxygen and nutrients, leading to cell death.
Causes: Ischemic stroke is caused by blocked blood vessels (often due to clots), while hemorrhagic stroke results from bleeding in the brain. Risk factors include high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, and heart disease.
Prevention: Managing blood pressure, maintaining a healthy lifestyle, controlling diabetes and cholesterol, avoiding smoking, and regular medical checkups.
Treatment: Emergency treatment includes clot-dissolving medications or procedures to restore blood flow in ischemic stroke, and surgical or medical management for hemorrhagic stroke.
When to see a doctor: Immediately if symptoms such as sudden weakness, confusion, difficulty speaking, vision problems, or severe headache occur.
Sources: World Health Organization (WHO), American Stroke Association, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Overview: A fluid-filled sac that forms near the tailbone, often containing hair and skin debris. It can become infected, leading to pain, swelling, and drainage.
Causes: Believed to result from hair penetrating the skin, leading to a foreign body reaction. Risk factors include prolonged sitting, friction, and excess body hair.
Prevention: Maintaining good hygiene, avoiding prolonged sitting, and keeping the area clean and hair-free may reduce risk.
Treatment: Treatment may include drainage of the cyst, antibiotics if infected, and surgical removal in recurrent or severe cases.
When to see a doctor: If there is pain, swelling, redness, or discharge near the tailbone area.
Sources: National Health Service (NHS), Cleveland Clinic, American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons

Overview: A severe injury caused by prolonged pressure on the body or a body part, potentially leading to muscle damage, tissue death, and systemic complications such as crush syndrome.
Causes: Heavy objects compressing the body during accidents, disasters, or industrial incidents.
Prevention: Following safety protocols in high-risk environments and using protective equipment.
Treatment: Emergency care including fluid resuscitation, monitoring for complications, surgical intervention, and supportive treatment.
When to see a doctor: Immediately after any significant crushing injury, especially if there is severe pain, swelling, or signs of shock.
Sources: World Health Organization (WHO), American College of Emergency Physicians, MedlinePlus

Overview: A neurological disorder characterized by the accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain's ventricles, leading to symptoms such as walking difficulties, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence.
Causes: Often idiopathic (unknown cause), but may be associated with prior brain injury, bleeding, infection, or surgery.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Placement of a shunt to drain excess fluid from the brain is the most common treatment.
When to see a doctor: If there are symptoms such as difficulty walking, memory problems, or loss of bladder control, especially in older adults.
Sources: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A condition involving hair loss from the scalp or other parts of the body, which can be temporary or permanent depending on the type.
Causes: May include autoimmune conditions (such as alopecia areata), genetics, hormonal changes, medications, or stress.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Treatment depends on type and may include topical or oral medications, corticosteroids, or other therapies.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing sudden or patchy hair loss, or hair loss associated with other symptoms.
Sources: National Alopecia Areata Foundation, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: An autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks the thyroid gland, often leading to hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid).
Causes: Autoimmune reaction influenced by genetic and environmental factors.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Thyroid hormone replacement therapy to normalize hormone levels.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing fatigue, weight gain, sensitivity to cold, or other symptoms of thyroid dysfunction.
Sources: American Thyroid Association, National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NHS

Overview: A condition in which the arches of the feet are flattened, allowing the entire sole to touch the ground when standing.
Causes: Can be due to genetics, injury, aging, or conditions affecting tendons or ligaments.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Supportive footwear, orthotic devices, physical therapy, and in severe cases surgery.
When to see a doctor: If foot pain, swelling, or difficulty walking occurs.
Sources: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A form of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease characterized by fat accumulation in the liver along with inflammation and liver cell damage.
Causes: Associated with obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome.
Prevention: Maintaining a healthy weight, balanced diet, and regular exercise may reduce risk.
Treatment: Lifestyle changes such as weight loss and management of underlying conditions; no specific medication is universally approved.
When to see a doctor: If there are risk factors for liver disease or abnormal liver tests.
Sources: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), American Liver Foundation, NHS

Overview: Bleeding into a joint space, most commonly affecting the knees, which can cause pain, swelling, and limited movement.
Causes: Injury, bleeding disorders such as hemophilia, or complications from surgery.
Prevention: Managing underlying bleeding disorders and avoiding joint injuries.
Treatment: Rest, ice, joint aspiration, treatment of underlying cause, and physical therapy.
When to see a doctor: If there is sudden joint swelling, pain, or reduced movement.
Sources: National Hemophilia Foundation, Cleveland Clinic, NHS

Overview: A condition in which pelvic organs such as the bladder, uterus, or rectum descend from their normal position due to weakened supporting muscles.
Causes: Childbirth, aging, menopause, chronic straining, or obesity.
Prevention: Pelvic floor exercises, maintaining a healthy weight, and avoiding heavy lifting.
Treatment: Pelvic floor therapy, pessary devices, or surgery depending on severity.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing a feeling of pressure, bulging in the vagina, or urinary or bowel issues.
Sources: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A break in one or more bones of the arm, including the humerus, radius, or ulna, often resulting from trauma.
Causes: Falls, direct impact, or accidents.
Prevention: Using protective gear and preventing falls.
Treatment: Immobilization with casts or splints, pain management, and sometimes surgery.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe pain, deformity, swelling, or inability to move the arm.
Sources: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A group of conditions in which the blood’s ability to clot is impaired, leading to excessive bleeding or bruising.
Causes: Genetic conditions such as hemophilia, vitamin deficiencies, liver disease, or use of certain medications.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Depends on cause; may include clotting factor replacement, medications, or treating underlying conditions.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing frequent or prolonged bleeding, easy bruising, or unexplained bleeding.
Sources: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: Bleeding within the skull, which can occur in brain tissue or surrounding spaces, potentially causing serious neurological damage.
Causes: Head trauma, high blood pressure, aneurysm rupture, or bleeding disorders.
Prevention: Managing blood pressure, preventing head injuries, and addressing clotting disorders.
Treatment: Emergency care, blood pressure control, surgery in some cases, and supportive management.
When to see a doctor: Immediately if symptoms such as severe headache, confusion, weakness, or loss of consciousness occur.
Sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A condition where there is an abnormally high level of potassium in the blood, which can affect heart function.
Causes: Kidney disease, medications, excessive potassium intake, or conditions causing cell breakdown.
Prevention: Monitoring potassium levels in at-risk individuals and managing kidney health.
Treatment: Medications to lower potassium, dietary changes, and emergency treatment if severe.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing muscle weakness, abnormal heart rhythms, or if diagnosed through lab tests.
Sources: National Kidney Foundation, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: An infection of the cornea (keratitis) that can lead to pain, redness, and vision problems.
Causes: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites, often associated with contact lens use or eye injury.
Prevention: Proper contact lens hygiene and eye protection.
Treatment: Antimicrobial eye drops or medications depending on the cause.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing eye pain, redness, blurred vision, or sensitivity to light.
Sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A localized collection of pus within the lung tissue, usually resulting from infection.
Causes: Bacterial infections, often due to aspiration of material into the lungs.
Prevention: Reducing aspiration risk and treating respiratory infections promptly.
Treatment: Antibiotics and sometimes drainage procedures.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing persistent cough, fever, chest pain, or foul-smelling sputum.
Sources: Cleveland Clinic, NHS, MedlinePlus

Overview: A mosquito-borne viral infection causing fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, and rash.
Causes: Infection with dengue virus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.
Prevention: Avoiding mosquito bites, using repellents, and eliminating breeding sites.
Treatment: Supportive care including hydration and pain relief; no specific antiviral treatment.
When to see a doctor: If high fever, severe pain, bleeding, or warning signs of severe dengue occur.
Sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Overview: Long-lasting inflammation of the sinuses lasting more than 12 weeks, causing congestion, facial pain, and reduced sense of smell.
Causes: Infections, nasal polyps, allergies, or structural issues in the nasal passages.
Prevention: Managing allergies, avoiding infections, and maintaining nasal hygiene.
Treatment: Medications, nasal sprays, and sometimes surgery.
When to see a doctor: If symptoms persist despite treatment or worsen over time.
Sources: NHS, American Academy of Otolaryngology, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: An abnormal growth of skin cells in the middle ear that can damage surrounding structures.
Causes: Repeated ear infections or poor Eustachian tube function.
Prevention: Prompt treatment of ear infections.
Treatment: Surgical removal is usually required.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing persistent ear discharge, hearing loss, or ear fullness.
Sources: NHS, Cleveland Clinic, American Academy of Otolaryngology

Overview: A condition where a part of the intestine twists around itself, causing obstruction and reduced blood flow.
Causes: Abnormal intestinal anatomy, chronic constipation, or previous surgery.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Emergency treatment including decompression or surgery.
When to see a doctor: Immediate care for severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or inability to pass stool.
Sources: NHS, Cleveland Clinic, MedlinePlus

Overview: Damage to bones, ligaments, tendons, or soft tissues of a finger due to trauma.
Causes: Cuts, crush injuries, fractures, or sports-related accidents.
Prevention: Using protective equipment and practicing safety.
Treatment: Cleaning wounds, splinting, medications, or surgery depending on severity.
When to see a doctor: If there is severe pain, deformity, bleeding, or loss of function.
Sources: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: Toxic effects resulting from excessive intake of pain-relief medications such as acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Causes: Overdose, accidental ingestion, or misuse of medications.
Prevention: Following dosage instructions and storing medications safely.
Treatment: Emergency care, antidotes (if available), and supportive treatment.
When to see a doctor: Immediately if overdose is suspected or symptoms such as nausea, confusion, or abdominal pain occur.
Sources: National Poison Control Center, FDA, MedlinePlus

Overview: An irregular and often rapid heart rhythm that can lead to blood clots, stroke, and other heart-related complications.
Causes: Heart disease, high blood pressure, thyroid disorders, or age-related changes.
Prevention: Managing risk factors such as blood pressure and heart disease.
Treatment: Medications, cardioversion, ablation procedures, or anticoagulation therapy.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing palpitations, shortness of breath, fatigue, or dizziness.
Sources: American Heart Association, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A common intestinal infection caused by small parasitic worms, especially in children.
Causes: Ingestion of pinworm eggs through contaminated hands, surfaces, or food.
Prevention: Good hygiene, frequent handwashing, and cleaning of living spaces.
Treatment: Antiparasitic medications and hygiene measures.
When to see a doctor: If there is persistent itching around the anus or signs of infection.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), NHS

Overview: A congenital condition in males where abnormal flaps of tissue in the urethra obstruct urine flow.
Causes: Developmental abnormality before birth.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Surgical removal of the obstruction and management of urinary function.
When to see a doctor: If there are urinary difficulties, poor urine stream, or recurrent infections in infants or children.
Sources: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NHS

Overview: A break in the skin of the neck that may involve underlying structures such as blood vessels, muscles, or airway.
Causes: Trauma such as cuts, accidents, or penetrating injuries.
Prevention: Using safety precautions and protective equipment.
Treatment: Immediate wound care, possible surgery, and infection prevention.
When to see a doctor: Immediately for any deep or bleeding wound in the neck area.
Sources: American College of Surgeons, MedlinePlus

Overview: A rare disorder of the esophagus where the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax, making it difficult to swallow food.
Causes: Damage to nerves in the esophagus; exact cause often unknown.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Procedures to relax or open the sphincter, such as dilation, surgery, or botulinum toxin injection.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing difficulty swallowing, regurgitation, or chest pain.
Sources: NHS, Cleveland Clinic, National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)

Overview: Hearing loss caused by problems in the outer or middle ear that prevent sound from reaching the inner ear.
Causes: Ear infections, fluid buildup, earwax blockage, or structural abnormalities.
Prevention: Protecting ears, treating infections promptly, and avoiding insertion of objects into the ear.
Treatment: Depends on cause; may include medications, removal of blockage, or surgery.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing hearing loss, ear pain, or persistent ear symptoms.
Sources: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), NHS

Overview: A condition where an internal organ or tissue protrudes through a weak spot in the abdominal wall.
Causes: Weakness in the abdominal muscles combined with strain such as heavy lifting or chronic coughing.
Prevention: Maintaining a healthy weight and avoiding excessive strain.
Treatment: Surgical repair is often required.
When to see a doctor: If there is a noticeable bulge, pain, or signs of complications such as nausea or vomiting.
Sources: American College of Surgeons, NHS, Cleveland Clinic

Overview: A group of neurological disorders affecting movement, muscle tone, and posture due to damage to the developing brain.
Causes: Brain injury or abnormal development before, during, or shortly after birth.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Therapies, medications, assistive devices, and sometimes surgery.
When to see a doctor: If developmental delays, abnormal muscle tone, or movement difficulties are observed in a child.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), NHS, National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)

Overview: A pattern of cannabis use that leads to significant impairment or distress, affecting mental, physical, or social functioning.
Causes: Repeated use of marijuana influenced by psychological, social, and biological factors.
Prevention: I don't know
Treatment: Behavioral therapies, counseling, and support programs.
When to see a doctor: If substance use interferes with daily life, health, or responsibilities.
Sources: National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), NHS

Overview: A fungal infection caused by Cryptococcus species, often affecting the lungs or central nervous system, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.
Causes: Inhalation of fungal spores found in the environment, especially in soil contaminated with bird droppings.
Prevention: Avoiding exposure in high-risk environments and managing immune health.
Treatment: Antifungal medications, often for extended periods.
When to see a doctor: If experiencing persistent cough, fever, headache, or neurological symptoms.
Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), World Health Organization (WHO)

Overview: Strep throat is a bacterial infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A streptococcus). It causes throat pain and inflammation and is highly contagious.
Causes: Caused by Group A Streptococcus bacteria, spread through respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing, or contact with infected surfaces.
Treatment: Antibiotics (penicillin or amoxicillin) are the standard treatment. Pain relievers such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen help manage symptoms. Rest and hydration are important.
Prevention: Wash hands frequently, avoid sharing utensils or drinks, cover mouth when coughing or sneezing, and avoid contact with infected individuals.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor if you have a severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing, high fever above 38.3°C, or if symptoms do not improve within a few days.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, CDC, American Academy of Pediatrics

Overview: Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils, typically caused by viral or bacterial infection. It causes sore throat, swollen tonsils and difficulty swallowing.
Causes: Most commonly caused by viruses (adenovirus, rhinovirus) or bacteria (Group A Streptococcus). Spread through respiratory droplets.
Treatment: Viral tonsillitis resolves on its own with rest and fluids. Bacterial tonsillitis is treated with antibiotics. Severe or recurrent cases may require tonsillectomy.
Prevention: Good hand hygiene, avoiding close contact with infected individuals, and not sharing personal items.
When to see a doctor: Seek care for severe throat pain, difficulty breathing or swallowing, high fever, or symptoms lasting more than a week.
Sources: NHS, Mayo Clinic, WebMD

Overview: Pharyngitis is inflammation of the pharynx (back of the throat), most commonly caused by viral infections. It is one of the most frequent reasons for doctor visits.
Causes: Viruses (rhinovirus, influenza, EBV) cause most cases. Bacterial causes include Group A Streptococcus. Environmental irritants can also contribute.
Treatment: Viral pharyngitis is managed with rest, fluids and analgesics. Bacterial pharyngitis requires antibiotics. Throat lozenges and warm liquids provide symptomatic relief.
Prevention: Hand washing, avoiding contact with sick individuals, and not sharing drinks or utensils.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor if symptoms are severe, persist beyond a week, or are accompanied by high fever, rash or difficulty breathing.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, UpToDate, CDC

Overview: Infectious mononucleosis (mono) is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Known as the 'kissing disease', it causes extreme fatigue, sore throat and swollen lymph nodes.
Causes: Caused by Epstein-Barr virus, transmitted through saliva, shared drinks, coughing or sneezing. Most people are infected at some point in their life.
Treatment: No specific antiviral treatment. Rest, adequate hydration, analgesics for pain and fever. Avoid contact sports due to risk of spleen enlargement.
Prevention: Avoid sharing food, drinks or kissing infected individuals. No vaccine is currently available.
When to see a doctor: Seek immediate care for severe abdominal pain (possible spleen rupture), difficulty breathing, extreme weakness, or jaundice.
Sources: CDC, Mayo Clinic, American Family Physician

Overview: The common cold is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract, primarily affecting the nose and throat. It is the most frequent infectious disease in humans.
Causes: Over 200 different viruses can cause a cold; rhinoviruses are responsible for 30–50% of cases. Spread through respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces.
Treatment: No cure exists. Treatment is symptomatic: rest, hydration, decongestants, antihistamines, and pain relievers. Antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections.
Prevention: Frequent hand washing, avoiding touching the face, avoiding close contact with sick individuals, and disinfecting frequently touched surfaces.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor if symptoms are severe, persist beyond 10 days, or are accompanied by high fever, difficulty breathing, or chest pain.
Sources: CDC, Mayo Clinic, NHS

Overview: Influenza (flu) is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses. It can cause mild to severe illness and can lead to hospitalization or death in vulnerable populations.
Causes: Influenza A and B viruses are the main causes of seasonal flu epidemics. Spread through respiratory droplets when infected people cough, sneeze or talk.
Treatment: Antiviral drugs (oseltamivir/Tamiflu, zanamivir) are effective when started within 48 hours. Rest, hydration and fever reducers help manage symptoms.
Prevention: Annual flu vaccination is the best prevention. Hand hygiene, wearing masks and avoiding crowded places during outbreaks are also effective.
When to see a doctor: Seek immediate care for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, confusion, severe vomiting, or symptoms that improve then return with fever.
Sources: CDC, WHO, ECDC

Overview: COVID-19 is a respiratory illness caused by SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, first identified in 2019. Symptoms range from mild to severe and can affect multiple organ systems.
Causes: Caused by SARS-CoV-2 virus, spread primarily through respiratory droplets and aerosols from infected individuals, including asymptomatic carriers.
Treatment: Antiviral medications (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, remdesivir) for high-risk patients. Supportive care includes rest, hydration and fever management. Severe cases require hospitalization.
Prevention: Vaccination is the most effective prevention. Additionally: wearing masks, hand hygiene, ventilation of indoor spaces and avoiding crowded areas.
When to see a doctor: Seek emergency care for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, confusion, inability to stay awake, or bluish lips or face.
Sources: WHO, CDC, ECDC, NIH

Overview: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs, which may fill with fluid or pus. It can range from mild to life-threatening.
Causes: Bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae most common), viruses (influenza, COVID-19, RSV), and fungi. Community-acquired and hospital-acquired forms exist.
Treatment: Bacterial pneumonia: antibiotics. Viral pneumonia: antiviral medications and supportive care. Severe cases require hospitalization and oxygen therapy.
Prevention: Pneumococcal and flu vaccines reduce risk. Good hand hygiene, not smoking, and maintaining a healthy immune system are also important.
When to see a doctor: Seek immediate care for difficulty breathing, chest pain, persistent high fever, coughing up blood, or confusion especially in elderly patients.
Sources: American Lung Association, WHO, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes that carry air to the lungs. Acute bronchitis is usually caused by infection; chronic bronchitis is related to smoking.
Causes: Acute bronchitis is usually caused by viruses (same as those causing colds and flu). Chronic bronchitis is primarily caused by smoking and air pollution.
Treatment: Acute bronchitis: rest, fluids, honey and ginger tea, cough suppressants. Bronchodilators may help. Antibiotics only if bacterial cause is confirmed.
Prevention: Don't smoke, avoid secondhand smoke and air pollutants. Annual flu vaccination reduces risk of viral bronchitis.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor if cough lasts more than 3 weeks, produces bloody mucus, is accompanied by high fever, or if you have difficulty breathing.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, NHS, American Lung Association

Overview: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, usually due to infection. It causes facial pain, nasal congestion and discharge. Acute sinusitis lasts up to 4 weeks.
Causes: Viral infections (common cold) are the most common cause. Bacteria, allergies, nasal polyps and deviated septum can also cause sinusitis.
Treatment: Nasal saline irrigation, decongestants, pain relievers. Bacterial sinusitis may require antibiotics. Chronic cases may need corticosteroids or surgery.
Prevention: Treat colds promptly, manage allergies, avoid smoking, use a humidifier, and wash hands frequently to prevent infections.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for severe headache, high fever, swelling around eyes, stiff neck, or symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, AAO-HNS, WebMD

Overview: Otitis media is a middle ear infection, most common in children but can affect adults. It often follows a cold or upper respiratory infection.
Causes: Bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) and viruses. Eustachian tube dysfunction allows pathogens to reach the middle ear.
Treatment: Pain management with ibuprofen or acetaminophen. Antibiotics if bacterial, or watchful waiting. Ear drops for pain relief. Drainage tubes for recurrent cases.
Prevention: Vaccination (pneumococcal, Hib, flu vaccines), breastfeeding in infants, avoiding secondhand smoke, and prompt treatment of colds.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for severe ear pain, hearing loss, discharge from ear, fever, or symptoms persisting beyond 2-3 days.
Sources: AAP, Mayo Clinic, NHS

Overview: Eustachian tube dysfunction (ETD) occurs when the tube connecting the middle ear to the back of the throat fails to open and close properly, causing pressure and hearing problems.
Causes: Allergies, colds, sinus infections, altitude changes, and enlarged adenoids. Swelling and mucus can block the eustachian tube.
Treatment: Swallowing, yawning, or the Valsalva maneuver to equalize pressure. Decongestants, antihistamines, nasal steroids. Severe cases may need ear tubes.
Prevention: Treat allergies and upper respiratory infections promptly. Avoid flying with active congestion if possible.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks, significant hearing loss, severe pain, or recurrent episodes.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, ENT Health, WebMD

Overview: Eustachian tube dysfunction (ETD) occurs when the tube connecting the middle ear to the back of the throat fails to open and close properly, causing pressure and hearing problems.
Causes: Allergies, colds, sinus infections, altitude changes, and enlarged adenoids. Swelling and mucus can block the eustachian tube.
Treatment: Swallowing, yawning, or the Valsalva maneuver to equalize pressure. Decongestants, antihistamines, nasal steroids. Severe cases may need ear tubes.
Prevention: Treat allergies and upper respiratory infections promptly. Avoid flying with active congestion if possible.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks, significant hearing loss, severe pain, or recurrent episodes.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, ENT Health, WebMD

Overview: White blood cell diseases include conditions like leukemia, lymphoma, and leukopenia that affect the production or function of white blood cells, impairing the immune system.
Causes: Genetic mutations, viral infections (HIV, EBV), radiation exposure, certain medications, and autoimmune conditions can affect white blood cell production.
Treatment: Depends on the specific condition: chemotherapy, immunotherapy, bone marrow transplant, or medications to stimulate white blood cell production.
Prevention: Avoid known carcinogens, maintain a healthy lifestyle, and seek prompt treatment for infections. Regular blood tests for high-risk individuals.
When to see a doctor: Seek immediate care for recurrent infections, unexplained fatigue, easy bruising, swollen lymph nodes, or night sweats.
Sources: National Cancer Institute, Leukemia & Lymphoma Society, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Gastroenteritis is inflammation of the stomach and intestines, typically caused by viral or bacterial infection. Often called 'stomach flu', though not related to influenza.
Causes: Norovirus and rotavirus are the most common causes. Bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli, Campylobacter) and parasites can also cause gastroenteritis.
Treatment: Oral rehydration is the cornerstone of treatment. Clear fluids, electrolyte solutions, gradual return to solid foods. Antibiotics for bacterial causes in severe cases.
Prevention: Hand washing, safe food handling and preparation, drinking clean water, and rotavirus vaccination for infants.
When to see a doctor: Seek care for signs of dehydration, bloody diarrhea, fever above 39°C, symptoms lasting more than 3 days, or inability to keep fluids down.
Sources: WHO, CDC, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Food poisoning results from eating contaminated food. Symptoms appear within hours to days and usually resolve within a few days without treatment.
Causes: Bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria, Staphylococcus aureus), viruses, and toxins in contaminated food. Improper food storage and preparation are main risk factors.
Treatment: Rest and rehydration are the primary treatments. Oral rehydration solutions replace lost fluids and electrolytes. Antibiotics for severe bacterial cases.
Prevention: Cook food to safe temperatures, refrigerate perishables promptly, wash hands and surfaces often, separate raw meats from other foods.
When to see a doctor: Seek care for bloody diarrhea, fever above 38.6°C, severe dehydration, neurological symptoms, or symptoms in elderly, pregnant or immunocompromised individuals.
Sources: FDA, CDC, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, a small pouch attached to the large intestine. It requires prompt medical treatment, as a ruptured appendix can be life-threatening.
Causes: Blockage of the appendix opening by fecal matter, mucus, or a foreign body leads to bacterial overgrowth, swelling and infection.
Treatment: Surgical removal of the appendix (appendectomy) is the standard treatment. Antibiotics are given before and after surgery. Laparoscopic surgery is preferred when possible.
Prevention: No reliable prevention exists, but a high-fiber diet may reduce risk according to some studies.
When to see a doctor: Seek EMERGENCY care immediately for severe pain in the lower right abdomen, especially with fever, nausea and vomiting. This is a medical emergency.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, American College of Surgeons, NHS

Overview: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common disorder affecting the large intestine. It is a chronic condition that requires long-term management.
Causes: Exact cause unknown. Factors include abnormal gut motility, heightened pain sensitivity, gut-brain interaction changes, microbiome imbalances, and psychological stress.
Treatment: Dietary changes (low-FODMAP diet), fiber supplements, antispasmodics, laxatives or antidiarrheal medications. Psychological therapies (CBT) are effective for many patients.
Prevention: Manage stress, identify and avoid food triggers, maintain regular meal times, exercise regularly, and ensure adequate sleep.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, persistent vomiting, difficulty swallowing, or symptoms that wake you from sleep.
Sources: International Foundation for GI Disorders, Mayo Clinic, ACG

Overview: Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing long-lasting inflammation and ulcers in the digestive tract, primarily the colon and rectum.
Causes: Exact cause unknown. Involves an abnormal immune response to gut bacteria. Genetic, environmental and microbiome factors contribute.
Treatment: Anti-inflammatory drugs (5-ASA compounds, corticosteroids), immunosuppressants, biologics (anti-TNF therapy). Surgery (colectomy) may be needed in severe cases.
Prevention: No known prevention. Regular medical follow-up, medication adherence, and avoiding triggers (stress, NSAIDs, certain foods) help manage the condition.
When to see a doctor: Seek urgent care for severe abdominal pain, significant rectal bleeding, high fever, or signs of dehydration.
Sources: Crohn's and Colitis Foundation, Mayo Clinic, British Society of Gastroenterology

Overview: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection in any part of the urinary system. Most infections involve the lower urinary tract (bladder and urethra) and are more common in women.
Causes: Bacteria (primarily E. coli from the digestive tract) enter the urethra and multiply in the urinary tract. Sexual activity, urinary catheters and immune suppression increase risk.
Treatment: Antibiotics are the primary treatment. Commonly used antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin. Increase fluid intake.
Prevention: Drink plenty of water, urinate after sexual intercourse, wipe front to back, avoid irritating feminine products, and don't hold urine for long periods.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor promptly for burning urination, frequent urge to urinate, blood in urine, or pelvic pain. Seek urgent care for fever, chills, back pain or nausea.
Sources: Mayo Clinic, NICE, European Association of Urology

Overview: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a common condition in which the force of blood against artery walls is consistently too high. It is often called the 'silent killer'.
Causes: Primary hypertension: no identifiable cause, develops gradually. Secondary hypertension: caused by underlying conditions (kidney disease, thyroid problems, sleep apnea) or medications.
Treatment: Lifestyle changes (DASH diet, exercise, weight loss, reducing sodium and alcohol). Medications: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, beta-blockers.
Prevention: Healthy diet, regular physical activity, maintaining healthy weight, limiting alcohol, not smoking, and reducing stress.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor regularly for blood pressure checks. Seek immediate care for a hypertensive crisis: BP above 180/120 with symptoms like severe headache, chest pain or vision changes.
Sources: American Heart Association, ESC/ESH Guidelines, WHO

Overview: Migraine is a neurological condition characterized by recurrent intense headaches, usually on one side of the head, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound.
Causes: Exact cause unknown. Genetic factors play a role. Triggers include hormonal changes, certain foods and drinks, stress, sensory stimuli, sleep changes and physical exertion.
Treatment: Acute: triptans, ergotamines, NSAIDs, antiemetics. Preventive: beta-blockers, topiramate, valproate, CGRP antagonists, antidepressants. Lifestyle trigger management.
Prevention: Identify and avoid personal triggers, maintain regular sleep and meal schedules, stay hydrated, manage stress, and consider preventive medication if attacks are frequent.
When to see a doctor: Seek immediate care for 'thunderclap' headache (worst of your life), headache with fever and stiff neck, headache after head injury, or new headache after age 50.
Sources: American Migraine Foundation, International Headache Society, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health conditions, characterized by persistent, excessive worry or fear that interferes with daily activities.
Causes: Complex interaction of genetic, neurobiological, environmental and psychological factors. Stressful life events, trauma, and certain medical conditions can trigger anxiety.
Treatment: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is highly effective. Medications include SSRIs, SNRIs, benzodiazepines (short-term) and buspirone. Lifestyle changes and relaxation techniques.
Prevention: Regular exercise, adequate sleep, limiting caffeine and alcohol, stress management techniques, strong social connections, and mindfulness practices.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor if anxiety is interfering with daily life, relationships or work, if you are using substances to cope, or if you have thoughts of self-harm.
Sources: American Psychological Association, NIMH, NICE

Overview: Depression is a common and serious medical illness that negatively affects how you feel, think and act. It is characterized by persistent sadness and loss of interest.
Causes: Combination of genetic, biological, environmental and psychological factors. Brain chemistry imbalances, life events, chronic illness and certain medications can contribute.
Treatment: Psychotherapy (CBT, interpersonal therapy), antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs), or a combination. Lifestyle changes including exercise, sleep and social connection are important.
Prevention: Regular exercise, healthy diet, adequate sleep, social support, stress management and early treatment of depressive episodes to prevent recurrence.
When to see a doctor: Seek immediate help for thoughts of suicide or self-harm. See a doctor if symptoms persist for more than 2 weeks and interfere with daily functioning.
Sources: WHO, NIMH, American Psychiatric Association

Overview: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by elevated blood sugar levels resulting from defects in insulin secretion, action, or both.
Causes: Type 1: autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing cells. Type 2: insulin resistance combined with relative insulin deficiency, associated with obesity and sedentary lifestyle.
Treatment: Type 1: insulin therapy. Type 2: lifestyle changes, oral medications (metformin), GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, and insulin if needed. Regular blood glucose monitoring.
Prevention: Type 1 cannot be prevented. Type 2: maintain healthy weight, eat balanced diet, exercise regularly, avoid smoking, and manage blood pressure and cholesterol.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for increased thirst and urination, unexplained weight loss, extreme fatigue, or blurred vision. Seek immediate care for very high or very low blood sugar.
Sources: American Diabetes Association, IDF, WHO

Overview: Anemia is a condition in which you lack enough healthy red blood cells to carry adequate oxygen to your body's tissues, causing fatigue and weakness.
