Causes: Iron deficiency (most common), vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, chronic disease, blood loss, hemolysis, bone marrow disorders, or inherited conditions like sickle cell disease.
Treatment: Depends on cause: iron supplements, B12 injections or supplements, folate supplements, treating underlying conditions, blood transfusions in severe cases.
Prevention: Iron-rich diet (red meat, legumes, leafy greens), adequate vitamin C to enhance iron absorption, B12-rich foods or supplements especially for vegetarians.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for persistent fatigue, pale skin, shortness of breath, rapid heartbeat, cold hands and feet, or dizziness.
Sources: WHO, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, Mayo Clinic

Overview: An allergic reaction occurs when the immune system overreacts to a harmless substance (allergen). Reactions range from mild to severe (anaphylaxis).
Causes: Common allergens: pollen, dust mites, pet dander, insect stings, certain foods (nuts, shellfish, eggs), medications (penicillin), and latex.
Treatment: Antihistamines, corticosteroids, decongestants for mild reactions. Epinephrine (EpiPen) for anaphylaxis. Allergen immunotherapy for long-term desensitization.
Prevention: Identify and avoid known allergens, carry epinephrine if at risk of anaphylaxis, wear medical alert identification, and consider allergen immunotherapy.
When to see a doctor: Seek EMERGENCY care for anaphylaxis: difficulty breathing, swelling of throat, rapid pulse, dizziness, or loss of consciousness. This is life-threatening.
Sources: AAAAI, Mayo Clinic, NICE

Overview: Chickenpox (varicella) is a highly contagious viral infection causing an itchy blister-like rash. It is now preventable by vaccine.
Causes: Caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Spread through direct contact with the rash or through respiratory droplets. Very contagious before the rash appears.
Treatment: Symptomatic: calamine lotion, antihistamines for itching, acetaminophen for fever. Antiviral medication (acyclovir) for severe cases or immunocompromised patients. Avoid aspirin.
Prevention: Varicella vaccine is highly effective (2 doses). Avoid contact with infected individuals. Post-exposure prophylaxis with varicella immunoglobulin for high-risk contacts.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for high fever, severe headache, stiff neck, confusion, difficulty walking, shortness of breath, or rash with severe pain or warmth.
Sources: CDC, NHS, AAP

Overview: Measles is a highly contagious viral disease causing fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and a characteristic rash. It was nearly eliminated by vaccination but is resurging.
Causes: Caused by the measles virus (morbillivirus). Spread through respiratory droplets. One of the most contagious infections known.
Treatment: Supportive care: rest, fluids, fever management. Vitamin A supplementation reduces complications. No specific antiviral treatment. Hospitalization for severe cases.
Prevention: MMR vaccination (measles, mumps, rubella) is highly effective. Two doses provide about 97% protection.
When to see a doctor: Seek immediate care for difficulty breathing, severe headache, seizures, confusion, or any signs of complications such as pneumonia or encephalitis.
Sources: WHO, CDC, ECDC

Overview: Mumps is a viral infection primarily affecting the salivary glands, causing characteristic swelling of the jaw and cheeks. It is preventable by the MMR vaccine.
Causes: Caused by the mumps virus (paramyxovirus). Spread through saliva, mucus, or close contact with an infected person.
Treatment: Supportive care: rest, fluids, analgesics for pain and fever, soft foods if chewing is painful. Warm or cold compresses on swollen glands.
Prevention: MMR vaccine (two doses). Isolate infected individuals to prevent spread.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for confirmation and to rule out complications. Seek urgent care for severe headache, stiff neck, high fever, testicular pain or loss of hearing.
Sources: CDC, NHS, WHO

Overview: Malaria is a life-threatening disease caused by parasites transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It is preventable and curable.
Causes: Plasmodium parasites (P. falciparum most dangerous) transmitted by infected mosquitoes. Found in tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, Asia and Latin America.
Treatment: Antimalarial drugs: artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) for P. falciparum. Chloroquine for sensitive strains. Severe malaria requires IV artesunate and hospitalization.
Prevention: Antimalarial prophylaxis when traveling to endemic areas. Mosquito nets treated with insecticide, repellents (DEET), protective clothing, and indoor residual spraying.
When to see a doctor: Seek URGENT care for fever after travel to malaria-endemic region. Severe malaria is a medical emergency: altered consciousness, severe anemia, kidney failure.
Sources: WHO, CDC, Malaria Consortium

Overview: Tuberculosis (TB) is a serious infectious disease that mainly affects the lungs, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is one of the top 10 causes of death worldwide.
Causes: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread through the air when infected people cough, sneeze or spit. Latent TB can become active when immunity is weakened.
Treatment: Standard treatment: 6-month regimen of four antibiotics (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol). Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) requires longer and more complex treatment.
Prevention: BCG vaccination (partially protective in children). Early identification and treatment of active cases. Improved ventilation and living conditions. Preventive therapy for latent TB.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for persistent cough lasting more than 3 weeks, coughing blood, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, or fever. TB requires mandatory reporting.
Sources: WHO, CDC, Stop TB Partnership

Overview: Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes (meninges) surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency with high mortality if untreated.
Causes: Bacteria (Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae most common), viruses (enteroviruses most common), fungi and parasites. Bacterial meningitis is most severe.
Treatment: Bacterial meningitis: immediate IV antibiotics and corticosteroids. Viral meningitis: supportive care. Hospitalization required. Early treatment is critical to survival.
Prevention: Meningococcal, pneumococcal and Hib vaccines. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of bacterial meningitis cases. Good hygiene practices.
When to see a doctor: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES for sudden severe headache, stiff neck, high fever, sensitivity to light, rash that does not fade under pressure, confusion or seizures. This is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Sources: WHO, Meningitis Research Foundation, CDC

Overview: A heart attack (myocardial infarction) occurs when blood flow to a part of the heart is blocked, causing heart muscle damage. It is a leading cause of death worldwide.
Causes: Usually caused by a blood clot blocking a coronary artery, often at a site of atherosclerotic plaque rupture. Risk factors: hypertension, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, obesity.
Treatment: Emergency reperfusion: primary PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention) or thrombolysis. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, anticoagulants, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, statins.
Prevention: Manage risk factors: control blood pressure and cholesterol, quit smoking, maintain healthy weight, exercise regularly, manage diabetes, eat heart-healthy diet.
When to see a doctor: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY for chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to arm, jaw or back, shortness of breath, cold sweats, nausea or lightheadedness. Every minute counts.
Sources: American Heart Association, ESC, WHO

Overview: Myocardial infarction (heart attack) occurs when blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked, causing damage or death of heart tissue. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment.
Causes: Usually caused by a blood clot blocking a coronary artery at the site of an atherosclerotic plaque rupture. Risk factors: hypertension, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, obesity, family history.
Treatment: Emergency reperfusion: primary PCI (angioplasty) or thrombolysis. Medications: aspirin, anticoagulants, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, statins. Cardiac rehabilitation after recovery.
Prevention: Control blood pressure and cholesterol, quit smoking, maintain healthy weight, exercise regularly, manage diabetes, eat a heart-healthy diet.
When to see a doctor: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY for chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to arm, jaw or back, shortness of breath, cold sweats, nausea or lightheadedness. Every minute counts.
Sources: American Heart Association, ESC, WHO

Overview: Angina is chest pain or discomfort caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle. It is a symptom of coronary artery disease and indicates the heart is not getting enough oxygen.
Causes: Coronary artery disease (narrowed arteries due to atherosclerosis). Triggered by physical exertion, emotional stress, cold weather, or heavy meals.
Treatment: Nitrates (nitroglycerin) for acute relief. Long-term: beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, aspirin, statins. Lifestyle changes and risk factor management. Severe cases: angioplasty or bypass surgery.
Prevention: Heart-healthy lifestyle, control of risk factors (blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes), not smoking, regular exercise.
When to see a doctor: Seek immediate care for new or worsening chest pain, pain at rest, or pain lasting more than 15 minutes — these may indicate a heart attack.
Sources: American Heart Association, NHS, ESC Guidelines

Overview: Bladder disorders encompass conditions affecting the bladder including overactive bladder, interstitial cystitis, bladder infections, and bladder stones. They cause urinary symptoms that significantly affect quality of life.
Causes: Bacterial infections, nerve damage, muscle dysfunction, bladder stones, anatomical abnormalities, or in some cases unknown causes (as in interstitial cystitis).
Treatment: Depends on specific condition: antibiotics for infections, anticholinergics or beta-3 agonists for overactive bladder, physical therapy for pelvic floor dysfunction, surgery for structural problems.
Prevention: Stay well hydrated, maintain good hygiene, urinate after intercourse, avoid bladder irritants (caffeine, alcohol, spicy foods), treat infections promptly.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for blood in urine, painful urination, frequent urge to urinate, inability to urinate, or recurrent infections.
Sources: Urology Care Foundation, Mayo Clinic, NICE

Overview: Kidney stones are hard mineral and salt deposits that form in the kidneys. They can cause severe pain when passing through the urinary tract and may lead to complications if left untreated.
Causes: Concentrated urine allows minerals to crystallize. Types: calcium oxalate (most common), uric acid, struvite, cystine. Risk factors: dehydration, diet high in protein/salt/oxalate, obesity, family history.
Treatment: Small stones: increased fluid intake, pain relievers, alpha-blockers to help passage. Larger stones: shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), ureteroscopy, or percutaneous nephrolithotomy.
Prevention: Drink 2-3 liters of water daily, reduce sodium and animal protein intake, limit oxalate-rich foods (spinach, nuts), maintain healthy weight.
When to see a doctor: Seek care for severe flank or groin pain, blood in urine, nausea/vomiting with pain, difficulty urinating, or fever with pain (possible infection).
Sources: National Kidney Foundation, Mayo Clinic, EAU Guidelines

Overview: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a blockage of one or more arteries in the lungs, usually caused by blood clots that travel from the legs. It can be life-threatening if not treated promptly.
Causes: Blood clots (deep vein thrombosis) traveling to the lungs. Risk factors: prolonged immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, clotting disorders.
Treatment: Anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, or DOACs like rivaroxaban). Massive PE: thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy. Long-term anticoagulation to prevent recurrence.
Prevention: Early mobilization after surgery, compression stockings, anticoagulants in high-risk situations, staying active during long travels.
When to see a doctor: SEEK EMERGENCY CARE for sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, rapid heart rate, coughing blood, or loss of consciousness.
Sources: ESC Guidelines, American Heart Association, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Prostatitis is inflammation of the prostate gland. It can be bacterial or non-bacterial and affects men of all ages, causing urinary symptoms and pelvic pain.
Causes: Bacterial prostatitis: E. coli and other bacteria. Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome: unclear, may involve nerve damage, stress, or immune dysfunction.
Treatment: Bacterial: antibiotics for 4-6 weeks (fluoroquinolones). Chronic: alpha-blockers, anti-inflammatories, physical therapy, psychosocial support.
Prevention: Practice safe sex, stay well hydrated, avoid prolonged sitting, treat urinary tract infections promptly.
When to see a doctor: See a doctor for painful or difficult urination, pelvic pain, pain during ejaculation, or fever with urinary symptoms (which may indicate acute bacterial prostatitis — a medical emergency).
Sources: European Association of Urology, American Urological Association, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Cerebral edema is swelling of the brain caused by excess fluid accumulation. It can be life-threatening as it increases intracranial pressure and can compress brain tissue.
Causes: Traumatic brain injury, stroke, infections (meningitis, encephalitis), tumor, metabolic disorders (hyponatremia, liver failure), or high altitude.
Treatment: Osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline), corticosteroids (for vasogenic edema), controlled hyperventilation, surgical decompression (decompressive craniectomy) in severe cases.
Prevention: Prevent head injuries (helmets, seatbelts), prompt treatment of infections and stroke, careful fluid management in at-risk patients.
When to see a doctor: SEEK EMERGENCY CARE for severe headache, altered consciousness, seizures, vomiting, vision changes, or focal neurological deficits.
Sources: Neurocritical Care Society, UpToDate, Mayo Clinic

Overview: Intracerebral hemorrhage is bleeding within the brain tissue itself, a type of hemorrhagic stroke. It is a medical emergency with high mortality and disability rates.
Causes: Hypertension (most common), arteriovenous malformations, anticoagulant medications, trauma, amyloid angiopathy, or bleeding disorders.
Treatment: Blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulation, surgical evacuation in selected cases, intensive monitoring in neurological ICU. Supportive care and rehabilitation.
Prevention: Control blood pressure, avoid excessive alcohol, don't smoke, manage anticoagulation carefully, treat vascular abnormalities.
When to see a doctor: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY for sudden severe headache, sudden weakness, speech difficulty, vision changes, or loss of consciousness.
Sources: American Stroke Association, ESO, Neurocritical Care Society
